ENT Clinical Note – Teleconsultation  
Date: [not documented]  
Clinician: Dr. Smith  
Patient: [redacted]

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  • “Blinding” continuous headache for 3 days; no clear precipitant identified.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  • Sudden onset on waking three days ago; persistent since.
  • Ibuprofen gives partial relief (pain decreases from ~8/10 to ~5/10) but never fully resolves.
  • Worse with sudden standing or head movement; photophobia present.
- ENT symptoms:
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation: Denied.
  • Voice change/hoarseness: Denied.
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia, drooling: Denied.
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms: Photophobia; intermittent “shooting lights.” No nasal congestion, discharge, epistaxis, or sinus tenderness. No ocular discharge.
  • Stridor/noisy breathing, dyspnea: Denied.
  • Facial/lip/tongue/uvular swelling: Denied.
  • Ear pain/hearing changes: Denied.
  • Neck pain/swelling: Denied.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  • Occasional short-lived headaches previously; relieved by ibuprofen.
  • No prior hospital or emergency visits for similar symptoms.
- Allergies: None reported.
- Current medications:
  • Combined oral contraceptive pill – specific brand/dose not documented.
  • Ibuprofen (OTC) – dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Social context:
  • Lives alone; works from home. Missed 1.5 days of work due to headache.
  • Non-smoker; drinks alcohol socially (~once per week).

Objective:
- Observable swelling/distribution: None reported.
- Airway/breathing: No stridor or respiratory distress reported.
- Mental status: Alert; able to converse.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded (teleconsultation only).
- Presence of accompanying person: None (patient at home alone).

Assessment:
- Probable migraine-type headache vs. other primary headache disorder.
  • Sudden onset, unilateral predominance over right eye, photophobia, visual phenomena (“shooting lights”), family history of migraine (mother).
  • No red-flag ENT or neurological features elicited (no focal deficits, no fever, no sinus symptoms, no neck stiffness).
  • Need for in-person neurological and fundoscopic examination acknowledged.

Plan:
- Medications:
  • Prescribe stronger NSAID (name/dose/route/frequency not documented) to replace ibuprofen; instruct patient to take with food.
  • May take paracetamol concurrently (dose/route/frequency not documented).
- Follow-up / further evaluation:
  • Arrange face-to-face appointment with clinic support team for full neurological exam, fundoscopy, and blood pressure check.
  • Reassess suitability of current combined OCP if migraine with aura confirmed; discuss alternative contraception at review.
- Escalation / red-flags advised:
  • If headache becomes unbearable, changes character, is associated with vomiting, new neurological symptoms, visual loss, fever, or wakes her from sleep, attend Emergency Department (A&E) immediately or call the service for advice.
- Education / instructions:
  • Continue current OCP until review unless advised otherwise.
  • Take new medication with food; may continue ibuprofen until prescription collected if needed.
  • Keep hydrated, rest in dark, quiet room as required.

Quality checks:
• Missing but expected elements:   
  – Exact name/dose/frequency of prescribed NSAID and paracetamol.  
  – Detailed neurological exam, fundoscopy, and vitals.  
  – Formal headache diary or assessment of trigger factors.  
• Internal conflicts: None noted.  
• Transcript quality: Clear; no significant audio gaps affecting clinical data.
